posts.title: Building a theme system with CSS variables in Next.js
posts.excerpt: How to build a flexible multi-theme system using CSS custom properties and React context — no libraries required.

body.content: CSS custom properties (variables) are the most underrated tool in a frontend developer's arsenal. Combined with React context, they let you build a theme system that is fast, flexible, and requires zero runtime overhead.
Why not a library?

Libraries like Styled-Components, Emotion, or even Stitches add kilobytes of runtime JavaScript to solve a problem that CSS already solves natively. CSS variables update instantly, cascade correctly, and work with any styling approach — Tailwind, CSS Modules, inline styles, whatever you prefer.
The structure
The system has three layers: design tokens as CSS variables on :root, a theme map in TypeScript, and a React context that applies the chosen theme's values to the DOM.
The React context

The ThemeProvider reads localStorage on mount, applies the chosen theme's variables directly to document.documentElement, and exposes setTheme and toggleMode to child components. No re-renders required for color changes — the CSS variable update handles everything.
Multiple themes, same system

Because every color in the UI reads from a CSS variable, adding a new theme is just adding a new object to the theme map. No component changes needed. This is the power of separating data from presentation.
The best theme system is the one you forget is there — it just works, for every theme, everywhere.
Performance
CSS variable updates happen in a single paint. No JavaScript reconciliation. No virtual DOM diffing. The browser handles it natively. This is why theme switching feels instant — because it is.

content: No flicker on initial load when using localStorage + SSR
Works with Tailwind's dark: variant via the .dark class
Each theme can override any subset of variables

posts.title: GSAP scroll animations that actually feel good
posts.excerpt: Practical patterns for smooth, purposeful scroll-triggered animations in React without over-engineering.

body.content: Most scroll animations I see on portfolios fall into one of two traps: either they're so subtle you barely notice them, or they're so aggressive that the page feels broken. Good scroll animation has one job: direct attention to what matters, when it matters.
The golden rule
Animate things that benefit from animation. A heading appearing as you scroll to it is meaningful — the motion reinforces that this content is new. A button spinning on hover is noise.
Setting up GSAP with React
The critical thing in React is using gsap.context() to scope your animations and calling ctx.revert() on cleanup. This prevents memory leaks and stale animation state on route changes.
Easing matters more than duration
expo.out is your best friend. It starts fast and decelerates naturally — the way physical objects actually move. A 0.7s expo.out feels snappier than a 0.3s linear animation.
Duration is how long. Easing is how it feels. Get the easing right and the duration barely matters.

posts.title: Node.js API architecture for 2024
posts.excerpt: Rate limiting, structured error handling, input validation, and logging patterns I use in every production API.

body.content: I've built Node.js APIs for startups, agencies, and solo projects. After enough production incidents, you develop opinions. These are mine — battle-tested patterns that I now apply from day one.
Structured error handling
Every API error should have a machine-readable code, a human-readable message, and an HTTP status. Never throw raw Error objects — create an AppError class that serializes cleanly.
Input validation at the boundary

Validate every request before it touches business logic. I use Zod because it gives you TypeScript types for free from the same schema definition. The parse happens in middleware — if it fails, a 400 is returned automatically.
Rate limiting is not optional

express-rate-limit with a Redis store. Different limits for different routes — auth endpoints get stricter limits than read-only data endpoints. Apply it globally with a more generous default, then tighten specific routes.

content: Separate limits for authenticated vs anonymous

body.content: Your API is only as reliable as its weakest boundary. Most attacks target the boundary.

projects.title: E-Commerce Platform
projects.desc: Full-stack storefront with product catalog, cart, Stripe checkout, order management, and admin dashboard. Handles 10k+ SKUs.
projects.summary: A production-grade e-commerce platform built for a retail client. Supports 10k+ SKUs, multi-variant products, real-time inventory, and a full admin dashboard — built in 6 weeks from scratch.
projects.challenge: The client had an existing Shopify store that was expensive, hard to customize, and couldn't support their specific multi-warehouse inventory logic. They needed ownership of the stack.
projects.solution: Built a custom Next.js storefront with App Router for SSR/SSG, a Node.js/Express backend with Prisma ORM, and Stripe for payments. The admin panel is a separate React SPA with role-based access.
projects.outcome: Reduced monthly platform cost by 80%. Checkout conversion rate improved by 12% after optimizing the funnel. Page load times under 1.2s for product pages.

projects.title: Ops Dashboard
projects.desc: Real-time logistics monitoring with WebSocket updates, interactive charts, and role-based access control. 50k+ daily requests in production.
projects.summary: Real-time operations dashboard for a logistics company — tracking vehicle locations, delivery statuses, and fleet performance metrics. Handles 50k+ requests per day with sub-100ms updates.
projects.challenge: The ops team was working with spreadsheets and delayed email reports. By the time they knew about a delivery issue, it was too late to intervene.
projects.solution: Built a WebSocket-powered dashboard with Socket.io, Redis pub/sub for message fanout, and Chart.js for live-updating metric charts. Role-based access for drivers, dispatchers, and managers.
projects.outcome: Mean response time to delivery issues dropped from 45 minutes to under 3 minutes. Zero downtime in 8 months of production.

projects.title: REST API Boilerplate
projects.desc: Production-ready Node.js API starter with JWT auth, rate limiting, input validation, Swagger docs, and 90%+ test coverage.
projects.summary: A production-ready Node.js API starter kit that I open-sourced after using a similar pattern across 5+ client projects. Skip the boilerplate, start with architecture.
projects.challenge: Every new project started with the same two weeks of setup: auth, validation, error handling, logging, rate limiting. Time that should be spent on product.
projects.solution: Codified my best patterns into a single, well-documented starter. Includes layered architecture (router → controller → service → repository), Zod validation, structured JSON logging with Pino, and a complete test suite template.
projects.outcome: Used as the starting point for 3 client projects. Estimated 12-15 hours saved per project in initial setup.

projects.title: Blog CMS
projects.desc: Headless CMS with MDX content, tag system, full-text search, and Incremental Static Regeneration. Sub-800ms load time.
projects.summary: A fast, minimal headless blog for a tech writer. MDX content, tag taxonomy, full-text search, reading time estimates, and an RSS feed. Loads under 800ms globally.
projects.challenge: The client wanted to write in Markdown with custom components, needed SEO out of the box, and didn't want to pay for a CMS subscription.
projects.solution: Next.js App Router with MDX processing via next-mdx-remote. Content lives in a /posts directory as .mdx files. ISR regenerates pages when content changes. Built-in search uses a client-side index.
projects.outcome: Core Web Vitals: LCP 0.8s, CLS 0, FID < 10ms. 95/100 Lighthouse performance score.

projects.title: Task Manager
projects.desc: Drag-and-drop kanban board with real-time team updates via WebSocket, notifications, and user authentication.
projects.summary: A collaborative kanban board for small teams — drag-and-drop cards, real-time sync across users, notifications, and project-based workspaces.
projects.challenge: The team was using Trello but needed custom fields, time tracking, and tighter integration with their internal tools. SaaS options were either too expensive or too complex.
projects.solution: Custom kanban with React DnD, Socket.io for real-time sync (optimistic UI + server reconciliation), and a PostgreSQL backend with normalized board/column/card schema.
projects.outcome: Deployed for a 12-person team. Average task completion tracking improved by 40% in the first month.

projects.title: Analytics Dashboard
projects.desc: Data visualization dashboard with filterable charts, date range pickers, and CSV/PDF export. Built for a logistics client.
projects.summary: A data visualization dashboard for a logistics client — filterable time-series charts, KPI cards, date range pickers, and one-click CSV/PDF exports.
projects.challenge: The client had data scattered across 3 systems and was exporting to Excel weekly to build manual reports. Each report took 3-4 hours.
projects.solution: Built a dashboard that pulls from a single aggregated API endpoint. Chart.js for interactive visualizations, date-fns for range calculations, and jsPDF for on-demand PDF reports.
projects.outcome: Still in development — targeting 90% reduction in time spent on weekly reporting.
